content: Class II division 2 malocclusion is a dental condition characterized by upper front teeth that are retroclined, meaning they are tilted backward toward the roof of the mouth, and an increased overbite, also known as a deep overbite. This condition can lead to functional oral problems and may also affect the patient’s appearance. To address this issue, orthodontic treatment often involves the use of specialized dental braces, known as functional appliances. These appliances are designed to move the upper front teeth forward and can also influence the growth of the upper jaw, lower jaw, or both. Most functional appliances are removable, and this treatment approach typically does not require the extraction of permanent teeth. However, to achieve optimal results, additional treatment with fixed braces may be necessary. An alternative treatment strategy involves creating space to correct the position of the upper front teeth by moving the molar teeth backward. This can be achieved by applying force to the teeth using a headgear, which is a device that transmits force from the back of the head to a fixed or removable dental brace attached to the back teeth. Depending on the specific case, this treatment may or may not involve the extraction of permanent teeth. If the use of headgear is not feasible, the back teeth can be stabilized using bands connected to a fixed bar placed across the roof of the mouth or in contact with the front of the roof of the mouth. This approach often requires the removal of two permanent teeth from the middle of the upper dental arch, one on each side. The objective of this study was to determine whether orthodontic treatment that avoids the extraction of permanent teeth produces outcomes that differ from no treatment or treatment involving the extraction of permanent teeth in children with Class II division 2 malocclusion. To investigate this, a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases was conducted, including Cochrane Oral Health's Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase, covering studies up to November 13, 2017. Additional searches were performed in the US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register (ClinicalTrials.gov) and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform to identify unpublished or ongoing trials. International researchers involved in Class II division 2 clinical trials were also contacted. The selection criteria for this review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials (CCTs) that evaluated orthodontic treatments for correcting deep bite and retroclined upper front teeth in children. Two independent reviewers screened the search results to identify eligible studies. If trials had been included, data extraction and risk of bias assessment would have been performed. The plan was to use random-effects meta-analysis to analyze the data, express effect estimates as mean differences for continuous outcomes and risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes, and explore any clinical or methodological heterogeneity. However, no RCTs or CCTs were identified that assessed the treatment of Class II division 2 malocclusion in children. The authors concluded that there is no evidence from clinical trials to either recommend or discourage any specific type of orthodontic treatment for correcting Class II division 2 malocclusion in children. Conducting such trials is challenging due to the low prevalence of this condition, difficulties in recruiting participants, and ethical concerns related to randomization. Consequently, it is unlikely that this evidence gap will be addressed in the near future.
